articles.title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
articles.summary: A bizarre, heavily armored amphibian roamed the oceans 237 million years ago, despite the fact that modern amphibians cannot survive entirely in saltwater. Discovered in China, the giant salamander-sized creature may be the first known amphibian to have adapted to a fully marine existence.
articles.content:
A remarkable fossil discovery in China has revealed an ancient amphibian that lived entirely in the ocean, something no amphibian alive today is known to do. The unusual animal, named Gerrothorax maritimus, had a broad, flattened body protected by bony armor and was roughly the size of a giant salamander. Researchers believe it spent much of its life on the seafloor, waiting to ambush passing prey.

The discovery comes from an international team at the University of California, Davis, Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. Their findings, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, are based on two exceptionally well-preserved skeletons dating back nearly 237 million years to the Late Triassic period.

Both fossils were uncovered in China's Guizhou Province, in a region that was once submerged beneath an ancient ocean hundreds of miles from major landmasses.

"This area is part of an ecosystem that we've been looking at and trying to reconstruct," said study corresponding author Ryosuke Motani, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at UC Davis. "We've been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian, and it's a sort of very unusual member of the lineage."

The finding is especially surprising because amphibians are generally unable to survive in seawater. Among the more than 8,000 amphibian species living today, none are known to spend their entire lives in marine environments, and fewer than 2% have any ability to tolerate salt.

Mammals, reptiles, and birds, by comparison, all include species that can live entirely at sea without relying on land for food or fresh water. Until this discovery, scientists had never identified convincing fossil evidence of an amphibian with the same ability.

A Giant Armored Amphibian Built for the Seafloor

Because the two skeletons are so complete, researchers were able to piece together the animal's appearance and develop a clearer picture of how it lived.

Gerrothorax maritimus measured nearly three feet long, but its proportions were far different from those of a modern salamander. Rather than having a long, slender body, it was unusually broad and flattened, with a distinctive disc-shaped form.

Its body was also covered in thick bony armor, which may have helped protect it from large marine predators such as ichthyosaurs.

"If you think about today's amphibians, this animal is unusual because it's big," Motani said. "It's probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what's different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky."

The structure of its skull, together with its heavy armor, suggests that this ancient amphibian was an ambush predator. Instead of actively chasing its meals, it likely rested on the seafloor until an unsuspecting animal came within reach.

"They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in," said Motani, who noted that the hunting strategy resembles that of the wobbegong, a type of carpet shark that lives near the seafloor and captures prey using suction.

How Could an Amphibian Survive in Salt Water?

One of the biggest mysteries surrounding Gerrothorax maritimus is how it managed to survive in an environment that is hostile to nearly all modern amphibians.

The problem comes down largely to amphibian skin. Unlike the relatively waterproof skin of many other animals, amphibian skin allows water and gases to pass through it. This makes it useful for breathing and maintaining hydration, but also leaves amphibians especially vulnerable to the effects of salt water.

"That skin is permeable, and that allows the animals to use it for multiple purposes," said Motani. "They use it for respiration and water intake, so amphibians don't drink or breathe through the mouth because they can do both through the skin."

As a result, modern amphibians generally depend on freshwater habitats or environments close to them. A few species have developed limited salt tolerance, including the crab-eating frog. Even these animals can lose weight when exposed to brackish water and must eventually return to freshwater to recover.

The ancient Gerrothorax maritimus, however, may have evolved a very different solution.

Researchers suggest that its extensive bony armor restricted the movement of water through its skin. This protective covering may have reduced its dependence on absorbing water directly through the skin, allowing the animal to take in seawater through its mouth instead.

Under this proposed mechanism, water would have been absorbed through the digestive tract, while the animal's gills could have helped eliminate excess salt. Gills are known to have been present in members of the Gerrothorax genus, giving the researchers reason to suspect that this species possessed a more fishlike approach to managing its salt balance.

Together, these adaptations may explain how an amphibian managed to occupy an ecological niche that remains inaccessible to its modern relatives.

Fossil Evidence Points to a Fully Marine Lifestyle

The researchers also examined whether Gerrothorax maritimus truly lived in the ocean or whether its remains might have been transported there after death.

Several clues strongly favor a marine lifestyle.

First, the skeletons were recovered from sediments deposited in a deep marine environment. Their remarkable completeness also provides important evidence about where the animals died.

"Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom," said Motani. "But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived."

The preservation of such delicate skeletal structures suggests that the bodies were not carried long distances before reaching the seafloor.

To investigate further, the team analyzed the fossils' chemical composition, focusing on the relative abundance of different forms of strontium, known as isotopes.

The results closely matched the strontium isotope signatures expected in ocean water during the Late Triassic, providing another independent line of evidence that the animals inhabited a marine environment.

Taken together, the fossil preservation, geological setting, and chemical findings make a compelling case that Gerrothorax maritimus spent its life entirely at sea.

The discovery reveals an unexpected evolutionary path for amphibians, showing that at least one ancient species appears to have overcome the biological limitations that keep its living relatives largely confined to freshwater environments.

The research received funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

The finding has broad scientific significance, challenges existing knowledge about amphibian habitats, and is well-detailed with fossil evidence and scientific analysis, making it an inspiring advancement in natural history and evolutionary science.
articles.personality_title: Fossils reveal 237-million-year-old amphibian that lived entirely in the sea
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Amphibians today mostly live in freshwater or on land because their skin lets water and gases pass through, making it hard for them to survive in salty ocean water.

**What happened** – Scientists found two nearly complete fossils in China of an unusual amphibian named Gerrothorax maritimus. This creature lived about 237 million years ago and had a broad, flat body covered in heavy armor. It was about three feet long and likely spent its life on the ocean floor, waiting to catch prey.

**Impact** – This discovery is unique because no modern amphibians live entirely in the ocean. Gerrothorax maritimus shows that some ancient amphibians could adapt to salty seawater by having thick armor that protected its skin and possibly using its mouth and gills to manage salt. This challenges what scientists thought about amphibians’ limits and shows a rare example of full marine life in this group.

**What's next step** – Researchers will study these fossils more closely to understand how this amphibian’s body worked in the ocean. They may also look for other marine amphibians to learn if this was a one-time adaptation or part of a bigger pattern in ancient life.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Fossils of Gerrothorax maritimus reveal that some amphibians lived fully in the sea 237 million years ago, showing a surprising way they adapted to salty ocean life.

articles.personality_title_es: Fósiles revelan un anfibio marino de hace 237 millones de años
articles.personality_presentation_es:

articles.title: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting
articles.summary: The conflict in the Gulf is an opportunity for the US to test its autonomous mine-hunting systems.
articles.content:
Traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most dangerous trips a vessel can take.

Despite assistance from the US Navy, ships are still being attacked.

"To transit the Strait of Hormuz you need agreement between the captain and the crew to take the risk. You need war risk insurance. And the captain has to make the final decision," says Steve Cameron, a former merchant navy officer and maritime consultant.

Missiles and drones are a threat from the air, but under the surface mines may also be lurking.

"If you're a captain, you'd like to see evidence mines aren't present," Cameron adds.

Modern mines rest on the seabed and detonate when they detect an acoustic or magnetic signal, triggering a pressure wave that will break the keel of a passing vessel.

Others can rise through shallow waters or float, or be powered towards a target.

The technology itself is not difficult or costly, but the mere threat can stop a tanker fleet from sailing.

Ian McFarlane of French defence group Thales is a naval architect who knows mine warfare well. "Mines are a very cheap way of waging a naval war, as the Royal Navy is acutely aware," he says.

Finding sea mines has traditionally been the job of specialist mine-hunting vessels, with crews of around 80 sailors.

To keep humans out of harm's way, an increasing amount of the work is done by systems that are autonomous and monitored from the shore.

They might only need 20 personnel, working in shifts on land. With the recruitment and retention challenges facing Nato navies these highly-portable robot systems are very attractive.

Such tech has been under development for 20 years.

During the 2003 Iraq war the US Navy poked around the seabed looking for mines with a torpedo-shaped robot called the Remus 100.

Pinging around with sonar these little machines operated down to around 100ft depth and spared divers a difficult and dangerous task.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the use of autonomous robotic systems to safely detect and neutralize naval mines, reducing human risk and enhancing maritime security in a dangerous region. This represents a significant technological advancement with broad implications for naval safety and operational efficiency.
articles.personality_title: Robot vessels help find dangerous sea mines in the Gulf
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Traveling through the Strait of Hormuz is very risky because ships face attacks from missiles, drones, and hidden underwater mines. These mines can explode when they sense a ship nearby, causing serious damage.

**What happened** – The US is testing new robotic systems that can search for these mines without putting people in danger. These robots use sonar to scan the seabed and find mines. They are controlled from shore by fewer people, unlike older methods that needed large crews on special ships.

**Impact** – This technology makes the dangerous task of mine hunting safer and easier. It reduces the number of sailors needed on risky missions and helps keep important shipping routes open, especially in conflict areas like the Gulf.

**What's next step** – The US and other countries may use more of these robots in future naval operations. They might improve the technology to detect mines faster and work in deeper waters, helping protect ships worldwide.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Autonomous robot vessels are improving safety by finding underwater mines without risking human lives in dangerous waters.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des navires robots détectent les mines sous-marines dangereuses dans le Golfe
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Traverser le détroit d’Ormuz est très risqué car les navires peuvent être attaqués par des missiles, des drones et des mines sous-marines cachées. Ces mines explosent lorsqu’elles détectent un navire à proximité, causant de graves dégâts.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les États-Unis testent de nouveaux systèmes robotiques capables de chercher ces mines sans mettre les gens en danger. Ces robots utilisent le sonar pour scanner le fond de la mer et trouver les mines. Ils sont contrôlés depuis la terre par moins de personnes, contrairement aux anciennes méthodes qui demandaient de grandes équipes sur des navires spécialisés.

**Impact** – Cette technologie rend la tâche dangereuse de la chasse aux mines plus sûre et plus facile. Elle réduit le nombre de marins nécessaires pour ces missions risquées et aide à garder ouvertes les routes maritimes importantes, surtout dans des zones de conflit comme le Golfe.

**Prochaine étape** – Les États-Unis et d’autres pays pourraient utiliser davantage ces robots dans les opérations navales futures. Ils pourraient améliorer la technologie pour détecter les mines plus rapidement et dans des eaux plus profondes, aidant à protéger les navires partout dans le monde.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des navires robots autonomes améliorent la sécurité en détectant les mines sous-marines sans risquer la vie des humains dans des eaux dangereuses.
